en: His form is the non-dual bliss nourished by Vajravilāsinī; though it causes the mass of darkness within living beings to vanish by raising up the inner light,
it is the vessel of his own powerful, non-conceptual, supreme wisdom and compassion.
May that Lord of the Thunderbolt make you the ground for the majesty of his radiant Fortune.
I am generally sustained by that Lord,
for his words speak loudly of my own welfare, just as mothers speak to a poor man.
Moreover, through the instigation of the vajra women seen in dreams,
I shall open [the treasury] for the sake of sentient beings, like a casket of jewels.

Furthermore, for the satisfaction of the world, I shall plant the cluster of blossoms from the wish-fulfilling tree of the tradition, as correctly disclosed by my guru, with an unobstructed abundance of fruits.

In this context, since the wise generally do not engage in listening to the scriptures and so forth without hearing the subject matter and other such elements, the compiler, implying the subject matter and so on by the force of the circumstances, says: "Thus have I heard," and so forth.

In this context, the *Śrīsaṃpuṭatantra* consists of ten kalpas; its title is [the tantra] itself. Its subject matter (*abhidheya*) is the Blessed Lord Vajrasattva, who is the essence of the tantra of the fruit (*phalatantra*), and he is also the teacher (*deśaka*). Because it is the cause for the direct realization of that [subject], the tantra of the cause (*hetutantra*) and the tantra of means (*upāyatantra*) are also the subject matter. Thus, the relationship between the teacher and the taught, the relationship between the expression and the expressed, and the relationship between cause and fruit have been stated. Furthermore, the purpose (*prayojana*) is the realization of the meaning of the *Śrīsaṃpuṭa* by those to be trained (*vineya*).

The ultimate purpose, which has been implied, is the accomplishment of the Mahāmudrā, whose nature is that of the resultant Vajradhara, which consists of the single flavor of vajra-like great bliss, and which benefits the entire world. Thus it is said:
*Vyākhyāyukti* 2.1: "In this way..."
Those who explain the meaning of the sūtras must state the purpose, the overall meaning along with the connection between the individual topics, and the resolution of objections.

Thus, the purpose has been stated according to this principle. The summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) and so forth are to be explained. In that regard, in the first chapter, the two sequences consisting of the sequence of generation (*utpattikrama*) and the sequence of completion (*utpannakrama*) are introduced. In the second, the causal tantra (*hetutantra*)—which is the sequence of completion itself—is specified. In the third and fourth, the sequence of completion alone is elucidated through detailed exposition. And since these two sequences are to be taught and practiced only by one who has been consecrated (*abhiṣikta*), the consecration, which is a limb of the two sequences, is analyzed in the fifth [chapter].

For one who has obtained the empowerments of the conventional and ultimate truths, who desires to attain the state of Mahāvajradhara, and who possesses superior faculties, the very cultivation of the *utpannakrama* (completion stage)—which is the direct means for the *mudrāyoga*, the direct means for the accomplishment of the *mahāmudrā*—is finalized in the sixth [chapter].

However, for those with weak or middling faculties, the *utpannakrama* must be cultivated preceded by the cultivation of the *utpattikrama* (generation stage), the *kramākrama* (sequential and non-sequential), and so forth; thus, the cultivation of the *utpattikrama*, which is the direct means for the *utpannakrama*, is revealed in the seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth [chapters].

Thus, for the sake of accomplishing the desired goal of a beginner yogi who practices both stages, the verbal gestures (*vākchomma*) and other such auxiliary means for understanding the secret signs (*saṃketa*) of the nearby yoginīs are taught in the thirteenth, fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth [chapters]. In the seventeenth, the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and other meeting places are taught for the purpose of bestowing grace upon those who have understood the signs.

In that regard, for the sake of enjoying the pure object—which is either another person who has gathered there or the limb of means consisting of the cultivation of the two stages—the two stages and the purification of the aggregates and so forth have been clarified in the eighteenth chapter. Furthermore, because the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā does not occur without conduct even for one of such a kind, the Samantabhadra-conduct is elucidated in the nineteenth and twentieth chapters.

Following that, the generation stage (utpannakrama) described in the third chapter and the systematic arrangement of the specific locations of the channels (*nāḍī*) were well-established in the twenty-first and twenty-second [chapters]. For the purpose of meditating on the generation stage in this manner, the mandala-homa, worship, and so forth of the generation stage were prescribed in the twenty-third and twenty-fourth [chapters] for the sake of deceiving and liberating from the planets and other external [obstacles].

The four previously mentioned *chommās* and the expansion of ritual actions (*karmaprasara*), which serve as limbs of the means (*upāya*), have been explained in the twenty-fifth, twenty-sixth, twenty-seventh, and twenty-eighth [chapters]. In the twenty-ninth, however, the nature of the vajra and vajra-bell is described. In the thirtieth, the rosary and so forth [are discussed]. In the thirty-first, the transference of consciousness (*utkrānti*) is treated. In the thirty-second, mantras are collected as limbs of the means.

In the thirty-third [chapter], the arising [of the deity] is taught through the meditation on the generated maṇḍala (*utpanna-maṇḍala-bhāvanā*), by means of the miraculous transformations such as the nature of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), birth, awakening, and the turning of the wheel of Dharma. In the thirty-fourth, the offering (*bali*) is described as a limb of skillful means (*upāyāṅga*) for the purpose of pacifying obstacles and so forth. In the thirty-fifth, the cloth painting (*paṭa*) and the manuscript (*pustaka*) are treated as limbs of skillful means. In the thirty-sixth, the musical instruments and other items used by the yogins during the assembly of the gaṇa at the previously mentioned sacred sites (*pīṭha*) and so forth are proclaimed.

For one who has thus engaged and meditates without ceasing, there is no accomplishment of Mahāmudrā without an external mudrā; therefore, service to a woman of noble family (*kulavilāsinī*), which is the direct means for the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, is prescribed in the thirty-seventh [chapter]. Likewise, at the time of the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, the unsurpassed ritual for the crest-jewel of the lords of yogins is definitively established in the thirty-eighth.

The specific nature of this very Blessed One, who has attained the fulfillment of his own welfare, as well as his illusory manifestations, are indicated in the thirty-third chapter and specified in the thirty-ninth. These two—the fulfillment of one's own welfare and that of others—constitute the *phalatantra* (the tantra of the fruit). Since this entire supreme human goal (*parapuruṣārtha*) cannot be accomplished without the service of the *samaya* through the cultivation of the unsurpassed wisdom and means that have uprooted the entire web of conceptual constructions, the service of the *samaya* is revealed in the fortieth chapter.

Thus, having briefly stated the meaning of the entire tantra for the purpose of demonstrating its excellence—thereby establishing the connection of the tantra so that the commentator may easily explain it and the listeners may grasp it—the explanation of the word-meanings and so forth for the summarized subject matter will now be set forth as the occasion arises.

In this regard, the introductory section (nidāna), beginning with "In this way" (*evam*) and ending with the word "he performed" (*akārṣīt*), is placed at the outset; for when these [conditions] exist, the teaching proceeds.
Indeed, the complete assembly of time, place, teacher, and audience constitutes the cause (nidāna) of the teaching, since without them, the teaching is impossible. As it has been said:

The Teacher and the assembly as witnesses, as well as the place and time, are specified for those possessed of faith as factors for engaging [with the teaching], in order to establish its own authority. (7v/16)

Thus [it is said]. Herein, the authority for the compilation belongs to the compiler of the recitation (*saṃgītikartṛ*). In that regard, the Blessed One taught the Dharma exactly as he had realized it, whereby the benefit of infinite disciples was accomplished. Furthermore, there were other future disciples who would arise at that time; for their benefit, the Blessed One was questioned by beings empowered by the Blessed One himself, and it was established that "Thus have I heard" the Dharma should be compiled by me from the *Dharmasaṃgītisūtra*.

Thus it was said in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*. Therefore, the compiler (*saṃgītikāra*) compiled it in that very same way. Who is the compiler here? What is the purpose of this determination of names? Since his words are spoken by the very command of the Blessed One, these are indeed the words of the Blessed One; the compiler merely recites them. For this very reason, the name of the compiler is not mentioned even at the end of the tantras, because the Blessed One himself entrusted [the teaching] to the great assembly.

Nor should it be said by all that [the teaching] was received from the Teacher exactly as heard; for one speaks, while others who were not present there assent to it—this is what is called a "recitation" (*saṃgīti*). Furthermore, they say here that it is Vajragarbha because he acted as the requester (*adhyeṣaka*).
Moreover, it will be stated that, by the power of those to be trained (*vineya*), the Teacher himself may be the compiler (*saṃgītikāraka*).

Thus [it is said]. Therein, the particle *evam* indicates that the entire meaning of the tantra (*tantrārtha*), which will be explained without error and which stands as if before the mind, is present right here. Consequently, this very word *evam* becomes meaningful through its connection with the entire meaning of the tantra. And they declare that the meaning of the tantra exists as the constituent parts of the two syllables, by virtue of being composed of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). Having thus explained it generally by means of the word *evam*, he will explain it specifically; therefore, there is no redundancy. Thus, this single great sentence (*mahāvākya*) being present, it is called "one tantra."
"By me" (*mayā*) means by myself directly from the Blessed One, not through a lineage of transmission.

"Hear" (*śrutam*) means it was understood through auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) as regards the phrasing (*vyañjana*) and through mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as regards the meaning (*artha*); it was not personally realized (*sākṣātkṛta*) by me. By stating this, he demonstrates reverence for the Dharma, [implying]: "Because the Blessed One alone has attained all aspects (*sarvākāra*) of this [Dharma]."

Alternatively, even though they have attained realization, because they are free from conceit, they conceive of the teacher as the Instructor; thus, the mention of "hearing" is for the purpose of instructing that the Great Bodhisattvas listen—even the Tathāgatas themselves—with insatiable thirst for the nectar of hearing the Jewel of the Dharma, so what need is there to mention others?

Having thus introduced the subject in general, he now demonstrates it in detail, along with its causal basis, in due order, beginning with the words "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*). "One" refers to a certain particular, inconceivable distinction of time, brought about by the accumulation of manifold stores of merit and gnosis, which cannot be delimited by lunar days, constellations, and so forth. Furthermore, in this context, that [time] is designated as a "moment" (*samaya*) in the form of the fourth moment. The connection is: "At that one moment, the Blessed One dwelt in identity with that."
Alternatively, "at one time" means at a single moment; by this, he indicates that he has attained the gateway of inconceivable liberation (*acintyavimokṣamukha*).
Alternatively, it expresses his great learning (*bāhuśrutya*) by stating that "this was heard on one occasion, and that on another.
Alternatively, it demonstrates the rarity of this *Tantraratna* by showing that "this was heard at one very specific time, and not at other times."

The *bhaga* is that by which the four Māras are shattered; thus, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is called *bhaga*. As it is said in the *Vajraśekhara*: "Shattering is called *bhaga*, because of the shattering of the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*) and the others."
"And those afflictions are to be slain by wisdom; therefore, he is called Bhagavat.

Alternatively, "bhaga" refers to the qualities such as sovereignty and so forth, because they are broken forth (*bhañjanti*) by means of these [qualities]. As he will state later: "of sovereignty," and so on. One who possesses *bhaga* is "Bhagavat. Alternatively, he is "Bhagavat" because he has conquered (*bhagnavān*) the four Māras, who are the adversaries; here, the elision of the letter *n* is according to etymological rule (*nairukta*).

And all of them have gone to and realized that very suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena; they have come from suchness for the sake of the world by means of its pervasive radiation, and they speak to others in exactly that same way—thus, according to the rules of etymology (*nairukta-vidhi*), they are *tathāgatas*. Their body, speech, and mind consist of the transformation, enjoyment, and dharma bodies, and those very [three] are their heart (*hṛdaya*); Vajradhara is of one essence with that, because they are born from him and are of his nature.
In some manuscripts, the reading "hṛdaya" is absent due to a scribal error. Indeed, the Blessed One himself will explain this word "heart" (*hṛdaya*) as it is employed here in the fourth chapter.

That very [vajra] is the vajra because its nature is emptiness; she herself is the woman (*yoṣit*) because she is the cause of unsurpassed bliss. Vajragarvā is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
(Note: This includes a critique of scribes!)

And her very *bhaga* is the *dharmodayā*, because it is the transformation of that [the *dharmodayā*] and because its intrinsic nature is that [of the *dharmodayā*]. Thus it is said in the *Advayasamatāvijayatantre*:
"The Blessed One (*bhagavān*) is indeed the Buddha; therefore, passion is not defiled."

He dwelt within that [consort], who is triangular in nature because she is the essence of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas; who is the source (*udaya*) of the qualities such as the ten powers; who is called the lotus of the Goddess embraced as the supported (*ādheya*); and who is the supporting form (*ādhārarūpa*). The plural number is used because Vajragarvā is the embodiment of the gathering of all women.

And because of the power of those to be trained (*vineya*), there is the manifestation of the mandala of the Great Vajradhara, who resides within a peaked palace (*kūṭāgāra*) atop a vajra-jewel summit, situated upon a universal lotus and vajra, located within the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*) inside every single atom of all stable and moving entities throughout the infinite world-systems of the ten directions. Here, although the peaked palace as the supporting structure is not explicitly mentioned, it follows by implication that he is in a peaked palace situated on the *bhaga*. For example, when it is said, "The wealthy man lives in the city," it follows by implication that he is in a palace situated within the city.

However, it was not stated in that way for the purpose of including other meanings and to demonstrate the preeminence of the stage of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). For even the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) is of one single flavor with that. Alternatively, he dwelt within the wombs (*bhaga*) of the goddesses such as Locanā, who have the nature of the internal earth and so forth, as well as within the *dharmodayas* and the lotuses of the Emanation Body and others.

"Vijahāra" means that by various means, through body, speech, and mind, he has always captivated and won over the minds of sentient beings to be trained according to their diverse inclinations. "Then, from there, I heard it" connects with what precedes. It is not said that he "stayed," because in reality the Blessed One does not abide anywhere at all.

As for what he will explain—that the Blessed One resides in that realm together with all the consorts of the Tathāgatas—the underlying intention is that he remains there for an infinite duration of time. By thus demonstrating the Blessed One’s dwelling in these three locations, the Sahajakāya (Innate Body), which is inseparable from emptiness and compassion, is clearly revealed. And by means of that very body, the teaching of the Tantra is also shown to be of one single flavor with it.

Alternatively, the Blessed One—the Lord of all Tathāgatas, whose nature is great compassion, and who is indeed the Bodhicittavajra—is the Vajra of the heart, body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. His consort is the Mahāmudrā, the Blessed Lady of Great Wisdom, who has the alternative name Samantabhadrā. Her *bhaga* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

That Blessed One dwelt there, having become one with that [reality] through a state of total integration (*ekalolībhāva*), because he no longer perceives any distinctions whatsoever. Although he is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*), by virtue of his prior awakening, he remains among all sentient beings according to the principle of a servant (*kiṃkara*)—this is the meaning.
As it has been said: "Like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), he is unshakable by the winds of all conceptual thoughts."
"Even while remaining thus, he fulfills the hopes of sentient beings without exception;
for although the Protector is free from activity, through the force of the momentum of his past formations, the teaching proceeds by means of the mechanism of a revolving wheel."

Furthermore, as for the fact that other meanings of the syllable *evaṃ* and so forth have been taught here and in other tantras, that is merely another teaching intended for the acquisition of *dhāraṇī* by those to be trained (*vineyajana*). This is because one retains [the teachings] by depositing a great mass of meaning within a single syllable. Thus, it is also indicated that these are taught at the beginning of the tantra because they possess great significance and are supremely auspicious. However, their recitation here is not justified as being denotative of those [other meanings].

Because of the disruption of their mutual connection, and since that meaning must necessarily be found in other sentences as well, what is the point of this insistence on a specific interpretation? Thus, the excellence of time, place, and person has been described.

He speaks of the perfection of the assembly: "There, indeed, the Blessed One was in the midst of eighty *koṭi*s of masters of yoga (*yogeśvara*). Yoga is the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of wisdom and means; mastery (*aiśvarya*) therein is sovereignty (*vaśitā*). Because they have attained that, the masters of yoga are the great Bodhisattvas who are lords of the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvara*). They are mentioned at the beginning as a representative indication of their great number, for the purpose of singling out Vajragarbha from among his peers. However, these alone are not the entire assembly, because they are infinite, as he will state later.
Then, in the assembly, there were yogins and yoginīs, ḍākas and ḍākinīs, and eighty million bodhisattvas, who praised the saṅgha of the Tathāgatas in many ways.

The Blessed One, through his knowledge of the minds of others, perceiving that the assembly was capable of hearing [the teaching] as if from a casket, and observing that Vajragarbha was fit to make the request, smiled. Although he had not been urged, he did so with the intention of exhorting [Vajragarbha], indicating that "this subject matter of the King of Tantras is the domain of those beings whose wisdom is already opened. Recognizing that intention through his own opened wisdom, Vajragarbha proceeded to make the request; this is what is shown.

"Immediately" means without interval. "From the seat" refers to the lunar disc; it does not mean from the ground. This [instruction] is also a request for and training in [the teachings] for those who have not yet arrived. He states the request with the words "to hear," and so forth. Regarding "Lord of Knowledge" (*jñānendra*): "knowledge" is the perfection of realization, which is the awakening to all aspects of all phenomena through the excellence of having abandoned the afflictive obscurations and the obscurations to the knowable, leaving no trace of latent tendencies. In this context, "Lord" (*indra*) refers to one who has attained supreme mastery. By virtue of attaining that supreme mastery, he is the "Lord" because he is the crest-jewel of the circle of teachers, such as Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha.

Alternatively, the Tathāgatas such as Vairocana are the cognitions whose nature consists of the cognition of mirrors and so forth; he is their Indra, that is, their sovereign, because he is their progenitor. For this very reason, the intention of the petitioner—who addresses him as "Jñānendra"—is that you alone are the uncommon teacher for those like me.

The connection is that, by changing the wording from "O Vajragarbha, ask! to "with the desire to ask," one should ask. Furthermore, it should also be connected with "O great Bodhisattvas. The address "Aho" is used in the sense of "wonderful" (*āścarya*), because for listeners such as Vajragarbha and others—who are suited to hearing [the teaching] due to their state of being prepared—it constitutes a marvelous domain; thus, taking it as "wonderful," he addresses them. "Vajragarbha" means that emptiness-wisdom (*śūnyatājñāna*) is the "vajra," and it is that which is "internally established" (*garbha*) within him.

Having thus described the perfection of wisdom, he speaks of the perfection of compassion: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Compassionate One. He says "excellent, excellent" because of the extreme excellence of that great compassion. Fearing that they might think, "We are unfit for this profound Dharma," and suspecting that they have been addressed by the Blessed One with such a thought, he addresses them as "Great" in order to dispel their despondency through an intention directed toward the ears of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Because their resolve (*sattva*) is set upon the great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) compared to the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas and others, they are called "Great Bodhisattvas" (*mahābodhisattva*).

The qualities (*guṇa*) are the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth; their "aspects" (*ākāra*) are their bases. This indicates that because these [qualities] consist of wisdom and compassion—as stated by way of their non-duality—you too are authorized to hear this. Furthermore, it is shown that others who have become such as these are likewise authorized here.

Regarding the phrase "in all tantras" (sarvatantreṣu): because even the secrets contained therein will be explained here with complete satisfaction, he says "all of that," since the secret will be explained in many ways. "We have been praised for our fitness to hear the unsurpassed Dharma"—this refers to the passage beginning with "with great joy. Repeated prostrations are performed precisely out of such joy in order to demonstrate the absence of pride. "What? asks regarding the subject matter (*abhidheya*); "How? is a question concerning the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its modes.

Why is it that, while all phenomena are common [to all], their essential nature remains a secret because it is not an object for anyone? (18v/38) *Saṃpuṭodbhavā* is a form where the nominative singular ending has been elided. "How" (*katham*) is a question regarding the relationship between cause and effect. In that regard, in the *Saṃpuṭodbhava*, what would be the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and how would all those [be] tantras? "Tantra" (*tantra*) is a continuum (*prabandha*), and it is threefold. Thus it is said in the *Samājottara*: "Tantra is declared to be a continuum; that continuum is threefold."
The support and the nature, according to their distinct classifications, are as follows. He states the detailed explanation of the terms thus mentioned:
"The nature is the cause of form, and likewise the fruit is the indestructible."
The basis, the means, and the summary of the meaning of the tantra by means of these three.

The emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of phenomena is their own-nature (*svarūpa*), their primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and their form (*ākṛti*); these are not different in meaning—“own-nature” is the intended sense—and that is the cause. The "Cause-Vajradhara" is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). The meaning is this: that very Buddhahood which is naturally established, though smeared by the stains of beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), is itself the cause of Buddhahood characterized by the attainment of purity. Furthermore, if these were not luminous by nature, they would not become stainless when cleansed, like charcoal. This was stated by the noble Maitreya:
Although suchness is undifferentiated for all, when it has attained purity,
it is tathāgatahood; therefore, all embodied beings possess that as their embryo.

Therefore, the cause is the removal of adventitious stains, and the fruit characterized by the attainment of purity is the Holder of the Fruit-Vajra (*phalavajradhara*). That is said to be "unassailable" because it cannot be overwhelmed by the stains of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). "Assailing" (*saṃharaṇa*) means either completely taking away or the brief withdrawal [of the stains]. The means for attaining purity—the cooperative condition consisting of the generated and the generation stages—is called the "support" (*ādhāra*), because [the fruit] arises from and remains based upon that, just as a sprout [depends] on the earth.

And that means (*upāya*) is, at the time of the direct attainment of *mahāmudrā*, the practice to be described through the yoga of the *mudrā*. For that [practice], the *utpannakrama* (completion stage) is the direct means; for that, the *utpattikrama* (generation stage); and its branches are the ritual expansions, consecrations, and so forth. Thus, there is a summary of the meaning of the tantras to be explained in three parts: the causal tantra (*hetutantra*), the resultant tantra (*phalatantra*), and the means tantra (*upāyatantra*). Regarding "the *Samāja* and so forth," the *Samāja* is the subject matter (*abhidheyārtha*). For it is said in the *Samājottara*: [From the *Guhyasamāja-tantra*] *(Note: The Sanskrit provided in the source text appears to be a fragment or a corrupted citation from the *Samājottara* or *Guhyasamāja-tantra*.)*
The threefold body, speech, and mind is designated as "secret" (*guhya*).
"Assembly" (*samāja*) is explained as a gathering (*mīlana*) that denotes all Buddhas.

Because each possesses the nature of the three vajras by virtue of being the nectar of gnosis whose single flavor is emptiness, there is the threefold body, speech, and mind. It is "secret" because it is not within the sphere of experience of unworthy persons; it is to be concealed. Since it manifests for the sake of the world in the form of all Buddhas, its "assembly" occurs in the thirteenth stage of the Vajradhara, which consists of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); therefore, it is the designation for all Buddhas.

Likewise, there is Śrīsaṃvara. "Śrī" is non-dual gnosis; "śam" is bliss, because he has transcended the three realms. And "vara" refers to his supreme form of great bliss, which is non-dual and inconceivable. His conduct is skillful in manifesting various forms, such as those of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and others. Although all conceptualizations along with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) have been cast aside, he delights the Bodhisattvas who are lords of the ten stages by teaching the Dharma with a voice as sweet as that of the *kalaviṅka* bird. Through various emanations suited to the capacities of beings, he brings to maturity the entire multitude of sentient beings, from the lords of the stages downwards.

Liberating [beings], he dwells having directly realized great enlightenment—whose other name is Mahāmudrā and whose nature is the nirvāṇa that is non-abiding in both existence and peace—in a peaked pavilion named Ghanavyūhavajramaṇiśikhara and others, located in the Akaniṣṭha realm above the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
So too is Hevajra. (Hevajratantra)

By the syllable *he*, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is expressed, and the *vajra* is said to be wisdom (*prajñā*). Great compassion is that which acts for the benefit of the entire world, being a non-referential compassion. Furthermore, in this context, that wisdom is of the nature of innate great bliss (*sahaja-mahāsukha*), which is the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*). That too, because it has a single flavor with emptiness, is called a *vajra* just like emptiness itself. That very [wisdom], consisting of great bliss whose single flavor is emptiness and acting for the benefit of the entire world, is the Fourth Body (*caturthakāya*), Hevajra.

Thus, the Blessed One Śrī Vajrasattva himself, whose nature is the *phāla* [the ploughshare], is the subject of expression everywhere by virtue of being the essence of the *Samāja*, *Saṃvara*, *Hevajra*, and so forth; he is both the means (*upāya*) and the cause (*hetu*). The specific textual compositions designated as the *Samāja* and others are so called because they express him. Their *nidāna*—their primary cause—is the *Saṃpuṭa*, the causal tantra (*hetutantra*). For it has been stated immediately thereafter that only when this very [causal tantra] exists does the causal *upāyatantra* proceed, as it could not otherwise do so.

It is real, true, and non-erroneous because there is no subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against it. It is certain, being established by both valid cognition and authoritative scripture. For instance:
"One who possesses compassion applies himself to the means for the sake of eliminating suffering. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.134)
For it is difficult to explain that which is beyond the senses—the goal and its cause;
therefore, one should examine the cause of suffering by investigating through both reasoning and scripture.

According to this principle, [the nature of things] has been directly realized by the Blessed One through yogic perception—perception that is personally experienced, characterized by diligent, uninterrupted, and long-term cultivation. And it is precisely the perception of the Blessed Ones that is primary, because its object is reality in all its aspects; it is non-erroneous with respect to reality in every aspect due to its non-deceptiveness. For it is by means of this that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know all phenomena to be without defining characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). Nor does it follow that the knowledge of the omniscience-in-all-aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) would thereby become a substantial entity.
Because all phenomena are included therein, and because even that [omniscience] is devoid of intrinsic nature, it is fully awakened to by means of them. Thus it is said in the *Āryaprajñāpāramitā*:
"The characteristic of direct perception is the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*), and that is without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*) for the Tathāgata."
"Thus it was perfectly awakened"— this refers to the inference elicited by the teaching thereof. [Pramāṇavārttika 3.108] A treatise is not contradicted by established reasoning or by its own words;

"Whether seen or unseen, that is what is to be grasped"—according to this principle, it has been determined by recent [authorities] through scripture. This is the meaning: this is the meaning to be understood through the force of the word *nidāna*. Otherwise, how could there be the status of a *nidāna*, given that [the object] would be non-existent due to being sublated and indeterminate due to the absence of a means of proof? And this applies to those who are adhered to false views such as a self (*ātman*).

It is beyond the reach of Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha, and even for the Śrāvakas—who, having directly realized the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*), have abandoned the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*)—because the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) exists in its entirety [for them]. It is also beyond the reach of the Pratyekabuddhas, because a portion of the obscuration of the knowable still persists for them. Therefore, he explains the *Rahasyasaṃpuṭa* as being "consisting of wisdom and means" (*prajñopāyātmaka*). Wisdom is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the knowledge thereof, because it has the single flavor of emptiness.

Skillful means (*upāya*) is that which effects the welfare of the entire world without exception by taking great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as its object, and has the nature of innate great bliss (*sahaja-mahāsukha*). That whose self-nature (*ātma-svabhāva*) consists of those two—wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means—in a state of non-duality, is such [a being]. Its essential form is the "union" (*saṃpuṭa*), that is, the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*). And so it is said in the *Samājottara*: "The union of wisdom and skillful means is designated as 'yoga'."
(24v/50) That which is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), and the characteristic of existence (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*) is skillful means (*upāya*).

Regarding "arising" (*udbhava*): because from this [tantra] the qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) arise—surpassing those of the Śrāvakas and others—and because they are produced as the essence of the fruit-tantra (*phalatantra*), it is called "arising. It is neuter due to Vedic usage (*ārṣatvāt*). By this, he illuminates its status as the causal basis (*nidāna*). For this very reason, he says: "The *saṃpuṭa*, etc."

"Samādhi" is so called because by means of it qualities (*guṇa*) are correctly placed, maintained, and brought to full maturity; it is non-conceptualization (*avikalpanā*). However, this arises as being "placed in equipoise" (*samādhīyamāna*) through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) by way of the complete turning away of all distraction. For one whose mind is concentrated knows things as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*), and consequently, qualities arise for him; thus he expresses this by using the term "samādhi. For this very reason, he will later state the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), since it is precisely from the state of concentration that the [characteristic] is to be explained.

Therefore he says, "the meaning is this. This is the intended sense (*tātparyārtha*). "Arising" (*udbhava*) means "origination"—this is the explanation of the term's meaning; however, *udbhava* here does not end in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "that very arising" (*tad evodbhavam*). Alternatively, that very *saṃpuṭa*, by virtue of being a meditative absorption (*samādhāna*) and the removal of adventitious impurities, becomes the nature of the resultant Vajradhara—thus it is "arising" (*udbhava*), with the suffix *-ac* used in the sense of the agent. "Of such a kind" means distinguished by the aforementioned qualifiers.

Stable entities—such as the world-receptacle consisting of mountains, rivers, oceans, earth, and peaks—and unstable entities—namely sentient beings—arise from the totality of causes and conditions; such are "beings" (*bhāva*). Their "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is their own form, their essential self-nature (*ātmasvarūpa*); that which possesses this is "of that nature. Since there is no other intrinsic nature for stable or unstable entities, [the author] says: although stable things and so forth are perceived even by fools, the fact that their intrinsic nature is not perceived is due to a lack of familiarity with the aspect of reality (*tattvāṃśa*).

It is characterized (*lakṣyate*) in the sense that it is counteracted; this is the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) by which that which is being cultivated is [defined]. The meaning is as follows: just as impermanence and so forth, though they are states inferred [by logic], are directly realized through the very activity consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), so it is for this [cultivation] as well. In this explanation, the analysis of the compound is: "the casket (*saṃpuṭa*) and its arising (*tad-udbhava*) are the characteristic. Thus, he speaks of the system of the result (*phalatantra*), wherein the result arises from the cause. (26v/54) Now, the meaning of the words beginning with "all" (*sarva*) is as before.
The state of being the primary cause (*nidānatva*) belongs to the Blessed One’s teaching of the mantras and so forth. *Vajra* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Regarding the statement in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*, "The vajra is said to be emptiness": one whose mind (*sattva*) has that nature—consisting of great bliss and compassion—is Vajrasattva, the Holder of the Vajra. Since a cause accompanied by distinguished means brings about the fruit, he speaks of the Method Tantra (*upāyatantra*), beginning with the words "The secret," and so forth. "Secret" refers to that which is not within the sphere of Hari, Hara, and others, characterized by the maṇḍala and so on. It is called "instructional" (*aupadeśika*) because it comes into being through the act of instruction. By this, the meaning of the term "arising" (*udbhava*)—that which arises from this—is explained.

Alternatively, the meaning of the word *udbhava* (emergence) is as before. And since that [emergence] is obtained through the power [of the practice] precisely by virtue of being the means (*upāya*) for the mantras and so forth, it is expressed here by the word *udbhava*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the ritual expansions (*karmaprasara*), pledges (*samaya*), and so on are included. The meaning of the word *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) is as before. According to this interpretation, the analysis of the compound is: "the emergence from the *saṃpuṭa*, which is the *saṃpuṭodbhava*, and that is its characteristic."

This being the case, the two meanings—the "seal of the source of all tantras" (*sarvatantranidānasaṃpuṭa*) and the "characteristic of the emergence of the secret" (*rahasyodbhavalakṣaṇa*)—are explained by repeating the phrase beginning with "all" (*sarva*) twice in the ancient commentary as three meanings, based on the principle that "the seal" (*saṃpuṭa*) constitutes a single meaning. These three meanings, whose nature is wisdom and method, constitute the tantra itself; thus, because it primarily illuminates the unsurpassed aspect of method, its excellence is declared to be the meaning of the tantra.

For it is precisely the forms of all the Buddhas, characterized by the supreme state of union with Mahāmudrā, that will be explained here. Indeed, the aspect of wisdom (*prajñā*) is common to the Pāramitā vehicle; the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*) is [common] to the specific Yoga Tantras; but the bliss of Mahāmudrā is uncommon. However, by means of explaining the categories of the Yoga Tantra, the reality of wisdom (*prajñātattva*) will also be explained primarily.

The meaning is as follows: this was spoken by me, Vajrasattva himself, for the sake of those disciples who are to be trained, through the projection of the ripening of the latent predispositions (vāsanā) established by the intention to teach; it is expressed both as internal reality (antastattva) and as external reality (bahistattva). Because it was composed by the Supreme Person of valid authority (paramapramāṇapuruṣa), it is non-contradictory; therefore, one should not entertain doubt or error regarding it.

This very intention, although already understood by the term *aupadeśika*, is set forth here once again so that the world, which is somehow difficult to instruct, might gain conviction. Even though [the Buddha] was questioned by many bodhisattvas, he said, "Listen to the words of the Teacher," because of the preeminence of the requester; it is not, however, an exclusion of others.

It is said that, by means of the very cultivation of the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of all phenomena, one must uproot the defilements accumulated through a succession of births from beginningless time; and having first abandoned the grasping at ordinary aggregates, one should cultivate the deity through the stages of generation and completion. Thus he says, "First," and so forth.

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), which is luminous clarity (*prabhāsvara*). The "impurities" are the obscurations of afflictions and the known (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*); the "stain" is that by which the body is smeared. Having contemplated the emptiness of the eighteen constituents (*dhātu*) associated with those stains—having washed them like clothes, and having performed this washing because of the primacy of the [mental] state—one should meditate upon the deity; this is the remainder [of the sense]. For this very reason, he points it out: "the realm of form" (*rūpadhātu*). A "realm" (*dhātu*) is so called because it is the basis for the obstruction of form.

It is called *rūpa* because it manifests (*rūpayati*) or obstructs (*bādhate*) by way of admitting another into itself; it is called *dhātu* because it maintains (*dadhāti*) its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), such as white, yellow, long, or short. Thus, "form-element" (*rūpadhātu*) means that which is both form and an element. In the expression "by the form-element" (*rūpadhātunā*), the instrumental case is used for "form" due to Vedic usage. The word "thus" (*iti*) means "by the form-element in its own nature, [which is] empty from the perspective of ultimate reality. However, this does not mean that form does not exist even conventionally. The word "that" (*tasya*) refers to it. The particle "eva" has the sense of "just like" (*iva*).

The meaning is that the Guru should cause sound to be empty, just like the form-realm (*rūpadhātu*). Manifesting this [emptiness], he connects it with the subject at hand by means of the passage beginning with "the sound-element" (*śabdadhātu*) and so forth. "Mind" (*manaḥ*) refers to the mind-object, the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), because the object is indicated by the subject. In the same way, it should be stated accordingly in what follows. By the phrase "by the nature of the eye" (*cakṣurātmyeti*), [it refers to] those things which are empty of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

Consciousness—how could consciousness be non-empty in the midst of the empty sense faculty and the object of consciousness? The implication is that it is indeed empty. The mental faculty (*manas*) and the external sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are its objects; both of these are empty. He concludes with the words "therefore," and so forth. By the word "and" (*ca*), consciousness is included. By the word "also" (*api*) in "also the collection" (*api rāśakaḥ*), consciousness is likewise included. Mind (*citta*), the mental faculty, its objective domain, and the mental factors (*caitta*); by the word "also," their respective consciousnesses are included as well.

Alternatively, the five objects are form and so forth; the five [faculties] such as the seer are the sense organs directed toward those objects. The mental factors associated with the mind—the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, which are specific states of mind—constitute the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*), the sixth object. The mind, however, consists of the six consciousnesses of the objects and the mind-faculty (*manaindriya*). For the mind-faculty does not exist separately, like the eye and other faculties.

However, the consciousness that has just passed away is called the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) because it exercises sovereignty over the arising of the subsequent specific consciousnesses. Thus, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) have been explained: the eye-element, the form-element, and the visual-consciousness-element; and so on, up to the mental-object-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mind-element. Since the six consciousnesses are included within the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*), there are twelve bases (*āyatana*).

The sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), the sphere of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*), up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the sphere of the mind (*mana-āyatana*). The five sense faculties and the five objects are the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). The five sensory consciousnesses are the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). That which is other than those, as well as the specific mental formations (*vijñānaviśeṣa*), constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). The aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are indeed subdivisions of the aggregate of formations, which is a mental factor (*caitta*); they are mentioned separately because they are the root causes of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

In that regard, the experience of objects through the direct perception of the nature of objects—which are either pleasant, painful, or free from both—is called the experience (*anubhava*), the feeling (*vitti*), or sensation (*vedanā*) of consciousness. That mental factor by which the apprehension, recognition, and determination of the specific characteristics of an object, such as its broad base and so forth, are performed is called perception (*saṃjñā*), consisting of the apprehension of signs (*nimittodgrahaṇātmikā*).

Other than these, the mental factors such as volition (*cetanā*) and so forth are the formations (*saṃskāra*); thus the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have been explained in detail in the *Munimatālaṃkāra*.

Thus, it has been stated that all phenomena are indeed these eighteen constituents (*dhātu*), and that they lack intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) in reality. And so it is said in the *Dvikalpa* [Hevajratantra II.iii]:
"The sense faculty and its object, as well as the cognition of the sense faculty..."
The eighteen elements are proclaimed for the awakening of the yoginīs;
their intrinsic nature is primordially unarisen, being neither true nor false.
All yoginīs know everything to be like the moon reflected in water, according to their own wish.

Having understood this as it truly is, one might raise the following objection: "If the reality (*tattva*) of all phenomena is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then one falls into the extreme of non-existence; for one who contemplates emptiness in such a way, how can there be purity consisting of stainlessness? With the intention of addressing this concern for future generations, Vajragarbha—both to refute this objection and to demonstrate a mere portion of the yoga of the deity immediately following the teaching on emptiness—says, "Listen," and so forth. The "path" (*mārga*) is that by which, in whatever specific manner, one searches, contemplates, and meditates.

"Listen to that," thus it is connected with the word "so" (tathā). He states its qualification: "non-duality" (advaya) means the absence of duality (dvaya). Because it is "devoid of duality"—that is, devoid of the existence or non-existence of duality and so forth—"devoid" (varjita) means exclusion, which is to say negation; the meaning is not a mere absence.

Now, is it not the case that even "mind-only," which is devoid of duality and constitutes the middle way, is not mentioned in various *sūtrāntas*? It is not so. For the Blessed One taught mind-only by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), but it does not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because in another *sūtrānta* its lack of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva*) is established. As it is said in the noble *Ratnakūṭa* (the *Kāśyapaparivarta*):

For the mind, Kāśyapa, when thoroughly sought, is not found. That which is not found is not apprehended; that which is not apprehended is neither past, nor future, nor present. That which transcends the three times neither exists nor does not exist; that which neither exists nor does not exist is unborn. That which is unborn has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); that which has no intrinsic nature has no arising.

That which has no arising has no cessation; that which has no cessation has no inequality. For that which is free from [inequality], there is neither going nor coming, neither passing away nor rebirth. Where there is neither going nor coming, neither passing away nor rebirth, there are no conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*). That wherein there are no conditioned factors is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); that which is unconditioned is the lineage (*gotra*) of the noble ones (*ārya*).
This is the detailed explanation. It is for this very reason that it was stated in this same context:

"‘Impermanent,’ Kāśyapa, is one extreme; ‘eternal’ is the second extreme. Likewise, ‘it exists,’ Kāśyapa, is one extreme; ‘it does not exist’ is the second extreme. That which is between these two extremes—formless, invisible, baseless, non-manifest, non-conceptual, and without abode—this is called the middle way, the true discernment of phenomena."

And that *dharmadhātu* is formless (*arūpya*) because it cannot be personally determined as "this is that"; it is non-demonstrable (*anidarśana*) because it cannot be shown to others; it is non-abiding (*apratiṣṭha*) because it does not abide in the form of internal elements or sense-bases (*āyatana*); it is non-manifest (*anābhāsa*) because it does not appear as external elements or sense-bases; it is non-cognitive (*avijñaptika*) because it has transcended the nature of the elements such as visual consciousness; and it is called non-abode (*aniketa*) because it is not the locus of any afflictions such as passion in their entirety.

If, however, there were some ultimately real entity in the interim that consisted of the very nature of the mind, then how could attachment to it as "existing" or "non-existing," or as "permanent" or "impermanent," be an extreme? For it is not logical that mental engagement which conforms to the reality of things should ever fall into a state of non-foundation. Nor is any other mode of being possible for a thing apart from its nature as permanent and so forth, which could constitute the true reality of that thing.

If it is argued that even the apprehension "it does not exist" would not be an extreme if there were no intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of an entity in the middle [of existence], [we reply: as it has been said, the apprehension "it does not exist" is invariably concomitant with the apprehension of existence; for a negation cannot be devoid of an object (*nirviṣaya*). And it is stated in the *Āryasāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā*:
"The past is empty, the future is empty, and the state of arising, ceasing, and abiding is empty."
"There is neither existence nor non-existence, for all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. And it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna:
[Quotation from *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 15.10 (variant: *nāśrīyeta*)]
"It exists" is the grasping at permanence; "it does not exist" is the view of nihilism.
Therefore, the wise person should not rely upon existence or non-existence. Thus, even the grasping at the "middle" has been addressed by the venerable Āryadeva.
The conceptualization that is free from existence and non-existence is the Middle Way;
yet this adherence to the Middle Way is not the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of illusion.

Thus it is prohibited. Therefore, this supremely profound reality is inconceivable because of the absence of generality (*sāmānya*); it is inaccessible to discursive thought (*vitarka*) and unknowable because of the absence of particularity (*viśeṣa*). Since there is no possible nature of an object to be sublated other than that which consists of generality and particularity, it is difficult to comprehend.

Alternatively, because it is not an object of the knowledge consisting of hearing, reflection, and meditative cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-maya-jñāna*), the three terms correspond respectively to the logicians who delight in conceptual constructions such as "universals" (*sāmānya*) and so forth; to Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha; and to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) such as those outside [the Buddhist fold] who are free from passion. For this very reason, because it is not within their range, it is a secret (*rahasya*).

The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are equal to space by virtue of their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); they are similar to that very [space] and have become of a single taste through the abandonment of all obscurations. This is the sense: it is to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedya*) by all Buddhas alone. As he will say, "the domain of the Buddhas. And that is realized internally through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), not through apprehension, by means of supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*) which is free from the entire web of conceptual construction and in which no phenomena appear. As it is said in the *Satyadvayanirdeśasūtra*:
"O Devaputra, the ultimate truth is that which transcends the domain of the omniscient wisdom endowed with the excellence of all aspects.

By this, he refutes the perception [of reality] through apprehension, by establishing that it has completely transcended the state of being an object. Ignorance is the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); it is like "darkness" because it veils the vision of reality. Even the knowledge produced by the Pratyekabuddhas through cultivation—which arises from their practice—is accompanied by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) even though they have abandoned a portion of the obscuration of the knowable; therefore, even they do not fully know [it].

By this, the following has been stated: non-dual gnosis itself is the path to enlightenment, consisting of the yoga with the deity. To whom does this apply? He says: "In cyclic existence," and so forth. Cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is the continuity of births projected by afflictions and karma within the three realms. That very cycle is an ocean (*arṇava*) because it is difficult to cross due to its vastness and because it is surrounded by crocodiles and other creatures in the form of the afflictions, which are the primary cause of many calamities such as separation from the beloved and union with the unloved. For those for whom it is thus "terrible" (*saghora*), bringing great fear, there is "crossing over" (*uttīrṇa*), meaning the act of crossing.

In this context, for those whose minds have gone [to that state] and who possess the awakened superior lineage (*prabuddhottaragotra*), while their bodies remain in the midst of the ocean of saṃsāra, the yoga of the deity consisting of non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*) is said to be "to be characterized" (*lakṣya*), meaning it is to be defined in such a way as to be transcended. The meaning is that it is spoken by the Lords of Sages (*munīndra*) as long as saṃsāra endures. In the reading *lakṣa*, *lakṣa* means a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). He states that characteristic: "One should determine in the *lakṣa*. The characteristic is the essential nature (*svarūpa*). [The term] *lakṣaṇām* refers to those things which are to be characterized (*lakṣaṇīya*).

Objects are called "consciousnesses" (*vijñāna*) because they are cognized. The sense faculties are called "knowledges" (*jñāna*) because objects are known by means of them. These [faculties] are six. Regarding those eighteen elements (*dhātu*) which are the objects of knowledge, the meaning is that one should characterize—that is, discern through knowledge—the object to be known, the characteristic to be known, and its nature as non-dual knowledge, by means of the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*), because through the observation and investigation of these, there occurs the realization of the non-dual reality.

Then, for the yogin whose mind observes the movement [of consciousness] and whose thought discerns the knowledge of reality, the path—the way of the yoga of the deity consisting of non-dual gnosis—becomes manifest. (38bisr/79) By this, may awakening be attained according to one's own will.

He states the benefit (*anuśaṃsā*) for this yogin: "A thousand," and so forth. Having attained various thousands of favorable rebirths (*sugatim*) and [avoided] unfavorable states (*akṣaṇa*) in previous lives, and now—due to the mention of the aforementioned characteristics—contemplating the entire universe as empty through equanimity and single flavor (*ekarasa*), he attains only a succession of good rebirths even if he has not achieved [the highest] accomplishment (*asiddhi*). Therefore, the meaning is that one should attain this by one's own will. Having contemplated emptiness, for what purpose should one contemplate the deity? He says: "Emptiness," and so forth; and from that, emptiness...

Because it is completely pure, the field is the primary [basis], and the sowing of the seed in that natural body is praised; therefore, one who possesses the wisdom that discriminates phenomena should perform that [sowing]. The summary meaning is this: the sowing of the seed by a wise person in a body purified by emptiness brings about awakening.
Thus, the yoga of the deity whose nature is non-dual gnosis is to be practiced through the stages of generation and completion for this very purpose. — *Hevajratantra* Q.
The teaching of the Dharma by the Vajradharas relies upon two sequences: that which arises sequentially and that which has already arisen sequentially.

Therein, he indicates the *utpannakrama* (the stage of generation) as being of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), beginning with the words "the channel" (*nāḍī*) and so forth. The channel is the *avadhūtī*, which extends from the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) down to the jewel (*maṇi*) and as far as the soles of the feet. However, it exists in the form of a knot in the midst of those [centers] located respectively at the crown, head, throat, heart, navel, secret place, and the middle of the jewel—which are designated as lotuses, wombs (*bhaga*), and wheels (*cakra*), numbering four, thirty-two, sixteen, eight, sixty-four, and thirty-two respectively.

From the hollow of the knot at her head, by means of the *caṇḍālī* yoga—whether by the *caṇḍālī* yoga known as the *utpannakrama-vasantatilaka*, or by the *sahaja-caṇḍālī* yoga—the *bodhicitta* emerges, possessing both concealed (*saṃvṛta*) and manifest (*vivṛta*) forms. This seed, which is the very nature of the Lord and the Lady, the source of all the qualities of a Buddha, must be generated through one of the three yogas within either the jewel-knot (*maṇi-granthi*) in the center or the secret-knot (*guhya-granthi*). As it is said in the *Hevajra Tantra*:
[Hevajra Tantra II.iv]
"By means of the maṇḍala circle and so forth, and through the process of self-consecration,
one should generate the bodhicitta in its forms of both the absolute (vivṛti) and the conventional (saṃvṛti). The conventional is like a jasmine flower, while the absolute has the nature of bliss."
And again:
"The wisdom arising from the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), equal to space, is endowed with its means. (Hevajratantra I.viii.40r/83)
"For the three worlds are born therein from the nature of wisdom and means; the Blessed One takes the form of semen, and that bliss is known as the beloved. Furthermore:
"Hevajratantra (I.viii.51cd):
For this is the stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*), which consists of the wisdom of the Omniscient One. And again:
*Hevajratantra* (II.iii.25):
"By means of the mandala circle and so forth, one certainly attains continuity."

Regarding the phrase "accompanied by the means" (*sopāyānvitam*): it is accompanied by the means in every respect. This very state of being accompanied is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "the three worlds" (*trailokya*) and so forth. The "three worlds" (*triloka*) refers to those things that are dissolved and perish at every moment through conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*); these are body, speech, and cognition (*kāyavāgbodha*). That which possesses these is the "one who has the three worlds" (*triloka*), namely the sentient being (*sattva*). That itself is the "three worlds" (*trailokya*), where the suffix *yaṇ* is used in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*), just as in the term *sāmānya*, derived from *samāna*. It is like the intermediate distinction between semen (*śukra*) and bliss (*sukha*), or like the two deities who have entered into union (*samāpanna*).

But this is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Ultimate wisdom and means, however, belong to emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and compassion (*kṛpā*) alone. Self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), which is the self-consecration performed at the time of initiation and so forth—even that omniscient gnosis—is composed of nothing but these. It is called "luminous" (*prabhāsvara*) because it is free from the darkness of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); it is by nature intensely radiant, like a pure crystal.

The reality (*tattva*) whose nature consists of the five wisdoms, such as the mirror-like wisdom, which are the essence of the five Tathāgatas, abides in identity with the sixth, Vajrasattva, at its center; it shines, and thus it is the "Deity" (*deva*), namely the *bodhicitta*, the innate bliss (*sahajasukha*). This is also stated in the *Dvikalpa* [Hevajratantra I.viii]:
"The deity is *bodhicitta*."
The venerable Nāgārjuna also said:
"No deity other than Cittavajra is ever proclaimed."

It is unmanifest from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*) because of its emptiness; it is said to have a manifest form (*vyaktarūpin*) by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtyā*). [The root] *ṛdh* means "to increase. "Possessing the entirety of supreme and most excellent power" (*ardha*) means that its measure (*mātra*)—its totality—is the highest and most sublime; thus, the meaning is that it is endowed with all the most excellent supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). It is subtle because of its profundity from the perspective of ultimate reality; it is the domain of an intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass.

Conventionally, however, "manopama" means that whose form is like the mind (*bindu*); the meaning is that its nature is the mind. Regarding the phrase "in the center of the heart": for those practicing the yoga of Sahaja Caṇḍālī, because it is the essence, it is said to be "always" (*nityam*) in the center of the knot of the *mahāsukha*-cakra known as the heart; the sense is that while it dwells there at all times, it occasionally dwells within other cakras, but not at every single moment. "Jyotivantaḥ" means luminous (*jyotiṣmat*). Knowledge (*jñāna*) is "light" (*jyotis*) because it destroys the darkness of all obscurations.
For this very reason, because its radiance spreads as an unimpeded manifestation, it is "of great splendor" (*mahādyuti*).

Regarding "the end of twelve" (*dvādaśāntam*): because of their proximity, the term "end" (*anta*) refers to those [twelve] themselves; thus, by way of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), there are thirteen. Regarding "the end of nine" (*navāntam*): likewise, "ten threads" (*daśā tantu*) means that everything has the nature of a thread (*tantusvabhāvam*). "One" (*ekam*) refers to the location. These [locations], as appropriate, extending from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, emerge and pervade through radiation the twenty-four locations beginning with the syllable *pu*, which will be described below.

Regarding "in the center of the navel" (43r/89): the secret [place] is also called the navel; therefore, here, for one who meditates on the Yogacaṇḍālī in the center of the secret knot (*guhyagranthi*), [she] remains having specifically cast away all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) by means of the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Among the four channels of the *uṣṇīṣa*-wheel, the *avadhūtī* is the fifth, like a digit (*kalā*) consisting of a mere fraction. That which, like the serpent-king (*nāgendra*), spreads and pervades each wheel in the form of a coil (*kuṇḍala*) and a knot—thus it is "extensive" (*vistara*); "entirely" (*sakalā*) is the archaic reading (*ārṣa*).

It exists together with the *kalās* and the *nāḍīs*; yet, by piercing even that which is "with parts" (*sakala*), one who meditates on the *caṇḍālī* perceives the action as having attained a nature free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) through its distinctness within the center of the *vajramaṇi*, by way of the essence of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*).

To explain how that is so, he says: "In the womb," and so forth. "Situated in the vajra-jewel hidden within the womb" refers to the syllable. To explain how even this is so, he says: "Through the *dharmadhātu*," and so forth. It has been liquefied by the mind—which is the *dharmadhātu*—through the performance of yoga that has become stabilized. This should be understood to apply to other yogas as well. By means of these qualifiers, he reminds us of what was already stated—that this [syllable] possesses the nature of a seed—in order to confirm it. Thus he says: "the seed."

This is the explanation of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) according to the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*). Regarding the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), he indicates the application of the *vasantatilaka* through repetition as "the channel," and so forth. The seed-syllable residing in the hollow of the channel's knot is the black syllable *HŪṂ*, which is the nature of the Blessed One and is called "Spring" (*vasanta*). Regarding "half," and so forth: by the rule that "it is a half-measure, and that consonant is likewise a half-measure," the syllable *HA* is unstruck (*anāhata*) and supreme; it is excellent because it is mounted upon the vowel *A*.

Because the letter *a* expresses the non-arising of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanutpāda*), it is called "the form of the drop" (*bindurūpa*) since it is defined and characterized by the dot (*bindu*) situated at its head. According to the oral instruction, it is accompanied by the moon and the resonance (*nāda*).

He states its location: it "dwells" (*vasanta*) in the center of the heart; according to the oral instruction, it is the syllable *haṃ* in the center of the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*). Regarding the "twelfth end": by analyzing the compound as "that which has the twelfth among the vowels at its end"—excluding the four neuter vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*—it refers to the syllable *oṃ*. According to the oral instruction, it is accompanied by the moon and the resonance (*nāda*). Regarding "the ninth at the end": the Lord is at the end of the ninth; according to the oral instruction, that syllable *oṃ* is accompanied by the moon-dot (*bindu*) and the resonance. He states its location: it is established in the center of the navel; [the syllable] *aṃ*.

According to the oral instruction, there is *oṃ* in the middle of the throat. These four seed-syllables abide pervading the body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head. Piercing all the threads of the wheels, that single thread called the *avadhūtī* emerges from the center of the *vajra*, takes its place within the centers of the vaginas—the four lotuses—and remains in the middle of their pericarp as the *dharmadhātu*. It is the moon of the *bodhicitta* which has been liquefied; by means of that which has become stable, it is the "seed," as previously described.

The cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of these two—the stages of generation (*utpatti-krama*) and completion (*utpanna-krama*)—will now be explained. The connection with what follows is: "one should maintain the gradual movement and progression of that *bodhicitta*. Alternatively, when the mind, which has the winds as its vehicle, is rendered motionless through the practice of yoga, one abides in the stage of completion (*utpanna-krama*). Regarding this, there are nine gates: the eyes, the crown of the head, the nose, the ears, the tip of the tongue, the throat, the arms, the heart, and the base of the navel. However, one who abides in the stage of generation should maintain [the mind] by means of the implantation of the seed-syllable (*bījāropa*); thus he says.

"Of the two seeds of earth" means that for earth there are two seeds, namely two *hūṃ* syllables; "of its eyes" means one should visualize them in the two eyes. "Blazing" refers to the seed-syllable of fire, *kṣuṃ*, [to be placed] on the palate. "Of the seed-syllable of wind, space, and so forth" means the wind-seed *yuṃ*, which is purified by emptiness and the rest. "In the nostrils and so forth" means in the two nostrils and the two ears. "By the primary mind" means having the form of the principal consciousness (*pradhānacitta*). "Of the seed-syllable of the water of nectar" means:

The seed-syllable of nectar is *suṃ*, which is purified by water; that seed-syllable should be applied to the faculty of the tongue, for its power resides therein. Its designation is "Lord" (*īśvara*). Regarding "of the neck, delusion, and seed-syllables": at the neck, one should remember the seed-syllable *smryuṃ*, which is the purification of delusion. Regarding "from the two arms": at the two armpits, likewise from the afflictions, is the seed-syllable *hmryuṃ*, which is the purification of the afflictions. Regarding "the moving one": this is wind; its seed-syllable is *ymryuṃ* at the heart. Regarding "from the two legs": [the following applies].

By the word *paśu* is meant the female owl (*ulūkī*); in her, the seed-syllable *kṣmryuṃ* is placed at the navel and the root [of the feet], that is, at the navel and the root. "With the eight limbs of the seeds" means with the seeds distinguished by the eight limbs (*aṅga*). This remains the same even when the reading is *aṣṭāṅgena*. Regarding *aṣṭāṅgam*, it means that which has eight limbs; one should maintain that sequential movement, meaning one should protect it with armor (*kavaca*) and restrain it.

(47r/97) [Objection: But nine doors have been mentioned; how then are there eight limbs here? [Response: Because the nose and ears are treated as one due to their having a single seed-syllable (*ekabīja*), they are figuratively considered a single unit. In reality, however, there are indeed nine limbs, so there is no contradiction. Regarding the phrase "according to the rule" (*vidhimān*): the meaning is that in the sequence to be described, immediately after the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatābhāvanā*), one should visualize oneself in the form of Jñānaḍākinī and be joined with the deities produced from the seed-syllables in the eight limbs.

Thus, the bodhicitta—inseparable from emptiness and compassion—is practiced through these two stages. It is "pervasive" (*vyāpin*), meaning it is all-encompassing. How so? Because the entire world is pervaded by it through identity (*tādātmya*). As it is said in the *Dvikalpa* [Hevajratantra]:
"This very great gnosis is established within every body."

"The non-dual, yet possessing a dual form, the Lord whose nature consists of both existence and non-existence, remains pervading the stable and the moving; He appears as if having the form of *māyā*. What is that world? [The author] points this out with the words "beginning with the immobile" (*sthāvarādi*). The world consists of the receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*) beginning with the earth, and the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*). Where is that world-pervader perceived? He says: "the support," and so forth. That Lord is the support for the form of the world of sentient beings together with the gods and asuras beginning with Brahmā; wherever He moves, that is the *bhaga*, which is the *dharmodayā*.

As it will be stated in the fourth chapter: "The support should be triangular and of noble form," and the *bhaga* is the emanation-lotus and so forth. It is called *bhavana* because within it the *bodhicitta* comes into being (*bhavati*), that is, arises in the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). "The Lord" (*prabhu*) means that the very essence of *bodhicitta* is the lord who is capable of both creating and destroying.
As it is said: "He himself is the creator, he himself is the destroyer, he himself is the king, he himself is the lord."

This is because of the sacred teaching; however, it is not [the case that] God or others [are the cause], because they are contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, for that very agent, there would be karma and non-karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious.

He states for how long [this lasts] with the words "as long as" and so forth. As long as one remains within the body—which has been made the object of the natural ego-grasping (*prākṛtāhaṃkāra*)—by means of various obstructions; he points this out precisely with the words "perform" and so forth. And it is for the sake of the non-rearising of this very natural ego-grasping that the meditation on deity-yoga (*devatāyogabhāvanā*) is taught. Regarding the phrase "but yoga": yoga, however, is equanimity; it is the single equanimity of wisdom and compassion. Meditation (*bhāvana*) is the repeated practice over a long period, respectfully and without interruption.

"When that exists, [there is] what is called the 'action-body' (*karmadeha*). This means the body is either the effect or the cause of virtuous and non-virtuous karma. "Of such a kind" means it is possessed of defects such as the beginningless natural ego-clinging (*ahaṃkāra*). "Shattered" means that which was obstructed by the latent tendencies (*vāsana*) of defects is now destroyed. At that time, that very master, whose nature is *bodhicitta*, becomes the deity Vajradhara. For that yogin who consists of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), since the expansion and withdrawal [of phenomena] occurs spontaneously according to his will, how could there be any obscuration of karma or obscuration of afflictions?

[Objection: But if this is so, since he lacks agency (*kartṛtva*) and the like, how can he act for the sake of others? [Response: He says, "But his own power," and so forth. His own unique power is that which is exclusively established in the purity of all aspects and is utterly potent.

By means of this—by which, as long as saṃsāra lasts, he pervades the world with immeasurable emanation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) without interruption, and through various miracles such as teaching and so forth, he establishes those to be trained (*vineya*) according to their capacity in a happy rebirth and in the three vehicles, and he removes their misfortunes and the like.

If it is argued that this being so, he [the Bodhisattva] is still possessed of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), we say: no. Because of the words "color" (*varṇa*) and so forth. It is called "color" because it is described; its own nature (*svarūpa*) is empty, like space. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no conceptual proliferation for him. "From that" means from his own power.
If it is asked, "In that case, does he not fall at the end of *nirvāṇa* like a Śrāvaka?", he says: "no," [referring to the verse] "In *nirvāṇa*... (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 10ab).

By means of wisdom there is no abiding in existence, and by means of compassion there is no dwelling in quiescence; thus, he is non-abiding in both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa. He remains uninterruptedly until the end of *saṃsāra* in the state of nirvāṇa, which is the single nature of great bliss free from outflows (*anāsrava*) and all obscurations. For this reason, he is a "hero" (*vīra*). He is a hero because he is difficult to conquer by the opposing factors, which are like the defects of a lotus; and he is a hero because of his victory over them. However, unlike the *śrāvakas*, his mind is not terrified of *saṃsāra*, nor does he have the notion that he has attained a one-sided nirvāṇa. As it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna in the *Bodhicittavivaraṇa* (vv. 88–93): [The verses follow.]
More wonderful than the wonderful, more marvelous than the marvelous, is this:
having realized that all these phenomena are empty, one still engages with the fruits of karma.
For these have arisen in the mire of existence with the intention of protecting sentient beings; they remain unstained by the defects of that existence, just as a lotus leaf is by water.

For these sons of the Conqueror, such as Bhadra and others, have indeed burned the fuel of the afflictions with the fire of the knowledge of emptiness; nevertheless, they remain moistened by compassion.
The passing away and birth, the manifest enlightenment, the display of difficult feats, the crushing of Māra’s army, and the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
The Lords of the World, acting under the sway of compassion, manifest their descent from heaven, their entry into nirvāṇa, and likewise their departure from the home.
"By manifesting as reflections of Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Rudra, and others,
those whose intent is compassion dance through the means of training the world."

Whence is his heroism? Because he has emerged from "lepa" (stain), which is to say, from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and is free from the impurities of the two obscurations. The neuter gender is used in the sense of the *ṛṣi* [tradition]. Thus, the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-tattva*) has been explained. However, since that cannot be directly realized without the reality of the means (*upāya-tattva*), he says "the mother," and so forth, in order to show how it is to be realized by employing those means through reliance upon the Vajrayāna. In this context, the "mother" is the one who bestows the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

The "sister" is one who has mounted the Vajrayāna. Some say that by the words "mother" and so forth, those who occupy the positions of mother and so on are meant; the Gurus, however, maintain that for practitioners of superior capacity, this is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*). But he himself will explain the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*): *prajñā* is the Yoginī whose form is emptiness, and *upāya* is Śrīvajradhara. Through the ritual application of these two, one should worship by means of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in the mudrā and in oneself. "One should worship" means one should satisfy those who desire [it]. As it is said: "By force, through union with the Yoginī, the yogi becomes one who has transcended gross transgression. (Kamalanātha, 52v/108)
Thus it is said; and as it has been stated in the *Hevajratantra* (I.x.6cd):
