"Wisdom (*prajñā*) is to be served for as long as she possesses semen (*śukra*)."

In this context, the reality (*tattva*) consists of wisdom and means; one who is devoted to that [reality] is its beloved, but not through passion and the like. "Effort" (*prayatna*) refers to the exertion in guarding [the secret]. "Disclosure" (*bheda*) means making it known. It is an inference made by oneself through the power of reasoning and the text. Furthermore, "disclosure" includes the disclosure of the mantra (*mantrabheda*). Disclosure of the mantra is the telling of it to another—either by oneself or with her as an assistant—due to intoxication, arrogance, anger, and so forth. Regarding non-guarding, the invisible fault (*adṛṣṭadoṣa*), such as falling into hell, is indeed well known. He also states the visible fault (*dṛṣṭadoṣa*):

By the words "agupte" and so forth: "agupte" means in the state of being unprotected or unguarded. Serpents, tigers, and the like; terrestrial beings such as humans and *piśācas*—these are the punishers. To the one desiring to know the reality (*tattva*), he says "mudrā" and so forth: here, the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra women belong to the family of Vairocana. "Amṛtavajrā" refers to the Kṣatriya woman, who is like nectar (*amṛta*) because she protects from the pains of injury (*kṣata-duḥkha*). "Karmakulajā" refers to one born of the Vaiśya family, whose lineage is primarily characterized by occupations such as trade. "Gopālikā" is the Śūdra woman. Here, "Mahāvairocana" is simply Vairocana himself.

Regarding the passage beginning with "in suchness" (*tathatāyām*): suchness (*tathatā*) is the state of being thus (*tathātva*). Because no specific quality of phenomena is designated, it belongs to all phenomena. Therefore, the reality of all phenomena as it truly is is called suchness. Furthermore, in the system of the *Pāramitās*, that is taught as mere emptiness; however, here, suchness is emptiness endowed with the specific means that will be explained. One who has gone (*gata*) into that is a Tathāgata, by the elision of the letter *ta*. The phrase "the glorious one, possessing both accumulations" is to be connected with what precedes.

And he has come in exactly the same way; as he went, so he has come. This is because that which consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) radiates forth for the sake of the world in the form of the five families and so on. By means of this *tathatā* (suchness), through the method of wisdom—which is non-different from supreme gnosis—and by way of identity (*tādātmya*).

For here, the universe is mind; and sentient beings—characterized by a continuum of mind and devoid of intrinsic nature—are the *tathāgatagarbhas* of the Tathāgatas. Furthermore, the entire treasure of the Dharma for the Tathāgatas consists of the five gnoses, such as the mirror-like gnosis and so forth. These are already naturally pure by virtue of their essential nature (*dharmatāśarīra*), yet they receive the designation of "five gnoses" and the titles of "Buddha" and "Bodhisattva" only upon the purification of adventitious obscurations, while abiding in their own true nature. Prior to that, however, they are designated simply as "seeds. Consequently, because they are the seeds of the Bodhisattvas, they are called "lineages" (*gotra*) and "families" (*kula*).

But if all Tathāgatas thus possess the five cognitions beginning with the mirror-like [cognition], and each of them possesses those five families beginning with the mirror-like [family], how then can there be a distinction of families? It is due to the distinction of lineages (*gotra*). For each of the [five] beginning with the mirror-like [cognition], the lineage of the shadow (*chāyāgotra*) is established for Bodhisattvas from time immemorial; however, the lineage of the shadow of the manifold [aspects] is the sixth.

Although there are many shadows, because each individual shadow is stronger than the others, they are subsumed under this or that family (kula) by imitating its respective nature; thus, he says "there are five," stating: "The family is said to be fivefold. Alternatively, it is introduced as follows: [Objection: But since other [families] not included within the five families would not be encompassed, the emanation (spharaṇa) would be merely partial. [Reply: No, for they are subsumed within the Sattva family.

[Objection: But in that case, the Sattva family would be the supreme one, because Vajrasattva is the sovereign lord of all. [Response: It is not so; for others also are born from him. However, due to a specific excellence, they are taught as belonging to a different family. But where such excellence does not exist, there is no basis for designating them by another name for their virtue, and thus they are designated solely by the Sattva family.

However, because the family of sentient beings—which conforms to those respective families—is subsumed therein, he says that there is a fivefold nature; namely, "the family is fivefold. And that, through conceptual elaboration (*prapañca*), consists of the five aggregates, the four elements, the five sense faculties, and the five objects, each having the nature of the five Tathāgatas, or else being distinguished by the peaceful, enriching, magnetizing, wrathful, and universal forms. Together with the five cognitions, such as the mirror-like wisdom, it is thus one hundredfold.

Even that, when divided, is infinite, endless, and incalculable—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "threefold": this threefold nature arises because those who conform to their respective families are subsumed therein. Thus, we shall explain with justification how the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*) is subsumed within the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśajñāna*), and the knowledge of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) within the investigative knowledge (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Alternatively, pride (*māna*) and envy (*īrṣyā*), which have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature, are included within the family of passion (*rāgakula*).

Or, because pride is based on delusion, it belongs to the family of delusion; or because slander and envy originate from hatred, they belong to the family of hatred. Yet all of this should be known as the single Vajrasattva family, as it will be said: "The family is declared to be fivefold, yet it is indeed one, the Śūnyavajrin. And in the *Samāja*, its nature is established as the indivisibility of the three vajras, beginning with:
"O noble ones, generate the mind in the form of the body," and so forth.

Furthermore, what are those primordial families (*kula*) from which other families will arise, and how are they called "families"? To this he says: "Of the families," and so forth. The five elements or the five aggregates (*skandha*) are the families. Because they are the very nature of the purity of those [elements/aggregates], and because they manifest initially as the form of the Vajra-holder (*vajradhara*), they possess primacy. And immediately after them, they exist in immeasurable forms.

As for that which is called their "family" (*kula*), the meaning is that it is so designated because those born from them are counted as a family (*gaṇa*) by virtue of that specific form. In this context, there are the five elements (*bhūta*)—earth, water, fire, wind, and consciousness—and the five aggregates (*skandha*)—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Furthermore, there are the "families of birth"; the meaning is that other families are produced from these.

[Objection: But in this way, the reality of emptiness (*śūnyatātattva*), accompanied by the means for knowing the object through the yoga of the mudrās, has been indicated; however, nothing to be cultivated (*bhāvya*) has been taught here, since there is only the instruction on the yoginīs of the five families who have already arisen in form, and likewise the indication for the yogins by means of the four gates. [Reply: True. In reality, because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are primordially quiescent, there is no arising of the object of cultivation, the subject of cultivation, or the act of cultivation; that is what he demonstrates with the words "there is no cultivator," and so forth.

Is the utpannakrama (the stage of completion) then simply the annihilation of both mantra and deity? To this he says: "These two should remain. Because they are of one flavor with emptiness, their nature is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); that nature consists of the innate great bliss (*sahajamahāsukha*). In that form, the mantra and the deity abide. He explains this very point with the words beginning "Vairocana," etc. *Ārolika* is Amitābha.

The meaning is that the reality whose nature is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca-svabhāva*) is expressed through the forms of Vajrasattva, Śiva, Amitābha, Sarva, Amogha, Vibuddha, Ratnasaṃbhava, Vairocana, and so forth. Since terms such as "Brahmā" are not well-known in one's own [tantric] system, he explains their meaning, beginning with "Brahmā. *Nirvṛti* means *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, in reality, the Buddha alone is Brahmā and no other, because [any other] is not liberated by its very nature. The same applies to the subsequent [terms] as well.

"Because of pervading" means because of its all-pervasive nature. "Because of being supremely auspicious" means because of its absolute auspiciousness. "The self of all" refers to one's own essential form (*nijam rūpam*). Since it abides there as a continuous stream (*santatyā*), it is therefore called "all. He says, "It is not even now known what its true nature (*tattvam*) is," meaning that which constitutes the essence of this entire universe. He explains: "By way of real bliss. Real bliss is the non-conceptual Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). "Awakened through the awakening to delight" means that precisely because of the awakening to that very Great Bliss, he is awakened; he is indeed a Buddha.

[Objection: "Surely the specific deities have been explained, but deityhood itself as a universal has not been explained. To this he says: "In the body" (*dehe*). [The term] *devatā* is derived from the presence in the body (*dehe sambhavati*), with the addition of the letter *va* and the elision of the suffix; thus, that very Blessed One (*bhagavān*) is so called. He says "Bhaga," etc. When the mind is thus purified, the qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), which are moistened by the essence of great bliss (*mahāsukha-rasa*), arise from their own seeds; therefore, these belong to him. He states the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the seals (*mudrā*): "The mother," etc.

"Jagaj-janam" means the noble world existing within the universe. "Vibhāgam" means the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. Having introduced [the subject] with the words "rajakī" and so forth, he explains it with the words "rañjanāt" and so forth. "Rañjanāt" means from causing affection.

For by means of wisdom, having understood the latent dispositions (*āśaya*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), all sentient beings are made to feel affection through appropriate practice; thus, wisdom alone is so described. Furthermore, because it milks the "cow of space" by producing qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), wisdom alone is so described. It is called "unwavering" because it does not abide in either cyclic existence (*bhava*) or nirvana. It is called "untouchable" because its single flavor is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

(60v/124) Even for these external mudrās, their status as *prajñā* is to be understood because they imitate these very qualities of *prajñā*. For this very reason, it is said that even through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in external mudrās whose nature is such *prajñā*, one who desires to know the reality of great bliss—the single flavor of emptiness—of the families of the Blessed Tathāgatas, should "serve" them; that is, they are to be cultivated.

Having established the deity in her manifested form, he speaks while establishing the mantra, beginning with "japam" and so forth. Because *ālikāli*—in the form of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*)—is the supreme mantra, he says "that is to be meditated upon" and so on.

[Objection: "In that case, if the flow of immeasurable states of mind is not ceased, there is only distraction and not meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); therefore, even the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) would not exist. To this, he says: "In the father," and so forth. That bliss is enjoyed by oneself, meaning it is experienced continuously through practice according to the instruction. Whether at the stages of youth, consecration, or otherwise—in the beginning, middle, and end—that bliss which is experienced without interruption is called meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

Thus, even when other [objects] after others are contemplated, because one recollects great bliss (*mahāsukha*) with an uninterrupted flow, from where could there be distraction? The intention is that, consequently, neither meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) nor its object (*dhyeya*) would exist. Alternatively, "in the father" refers to the guru; at the time of initiation, whatever innate great bliss (*sahajamahāsukha*) was obtained and experienced, that is enjoyed—that is, relished—by oneself at other times as well. Or, through union with the consort (*mudrā*), it is enjoyed in exactly that same way.

That happiness by which, when experienced, there would be death—the cessation of the sense faculties—is called "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*) in this very life, in this very birth. And such meditative absorption of one who has attained yoga is permitted even without explicit instruction, simply through effortless recollection (*anusmaraṇa*).

Thus ends [the section]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the armor-visualization (*kavaca*) and other such practices are included. A *prakaraṇa*—meaning a chapter (*pariccheda*) or a section (*paṭala*)—is so called because it is by means of this that the reality (*tattva*), which is the non-erroneous nature, of the meditations on the designation, the designated, the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and the words [of the mantra], is set forth (*prakriyate*) or introduced (*prastūyate*). It is not different in meaning from these terms, as it has been indicated at the beginning of the first [chapter] and so on.
The first cluster in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*, a commentary on the *Saṃpuṭa*, composed by the great scholar Abhayākaragupta.
